roles.name: Attorney for financial matters under an enduring power of attorney
roles.summary: An adult with decision-making capacity can appoint an attorney for financial matters in the prescribed form. The principal chooses when the power starts. It can start at once, when the principal loses capacity, or at another time or event. If the document says nothing, it starts as soon as the document is made. Loss of capacity does not end it, but death does. The attorney cannot run the estate after death.

assigned.event: Principal with decision-making capacity signs the prescribed form before two witnesses, one authorised to witness affidavits or a medical practitioner; the attorney signs a witnessed acceptance

starts.event: On the time, circumstance or occasion specified (e.g. immediately, or when the principal ceases to have decision making capacity). If nothing is specified, on the making of the power. If capacity is lost before a specified later start, the power becomes exercisable during the incapacity.

ends.event: Death of the principal
Principal (with capacity) revokes it, or makes a later enduring power of attorney (unless it says otherwise)
Revoked according to its own terms

As to that attorney: the attorney dies, loses capacity, becomes insolvent under administration, becomes a care worker/health/accommodation provider for the principal, is convicted of a dishonesty offence, or resigns
VCAT declares it invalid or revokes it

notes.text: Regaining capacity does not stop an attorney who began acting because of incapacity. The principal also keeps their own legal capacity to act.

Unlike Queensland, the Victorian Act has no provision revoking an enduring power of attorney on the principal's later marriage, divorce or end of a domestic partnership. Revocation events are those in Part 5 (ss 43-62).
There is no registration requirement before use. The Act requires only the prescribed form, witnessing and acceptance.

An attorney acting for a principal who lacks capacity must act in the least restrictive way, support the principal's participation and give effect to their wishes. Before first acting because of incapacity, the attorney must notify anyone the instrument names.

roles.name: Attorney for personal matters under an enduring power of attorney
roles.summary: The same enduring power of attorney can cover personal or lifestyle matters, such as where and with whom the principal lives. It cannot cover medical treatment, which is handled by a medical treatment decision maker under the 2016 Act. In Victoria, power over personal matters is not limited by statute to periods of incapacity: the principal sets the start, and the default is on making. It ends at death.

starts.event: As specified in the instrument (e.g. when the principal ceases to have capacity); otherwise on making

notes.text: Canonical mapping: this role is lined up with 'health-care-agent' because it is the appointed personal-welfare attorney. Medical treatment is excluded from 'personal matter' in Victoria and belongs to the appointed medical treatment decision maker.
Transitional rule: an attorney under a pre-2018 enduring power who kept power to make medical treatment decisions is taken to be the appointed medical treatment decision maker.

roles.name: Supportive attorney
roles.summary: An adult with capacity can appoint a supportive attorney. The supportive attorney helps the principal make and carry out the principal's own decisions on personal, financial or other matters, but not medical treatment. They may get information, communicate decisions and take steps to give effect to them. The appointment has no effect while the principal lacks capacity and is revoked at death.

notes.text: Powers are limited to information, communication and giving effect to the principal's own decisions. A supported decision remains the principal's decision.

roles.name: Appointed medical treatment decision maker
roles.summary: An adult with capacity may appoint one or more medical treatment decision makers. The appointment is in force from the date it is made, but it gives no decision-making power while the person can decide. It is used only when the person lacks decision-making capacity for the treatment decision. The appointee then makes the decision the person would have made. It ranks first in the statutory hierarchy.

assigned.event: Adult with capacity signs a written appointment, witnessed and certified; each appointee signs a witnessed acceptance

starts.event: Appointment is in force on the date made, but the power to decide arises only when the person does not have decision-making capacity for the particular treatment decision

ends.event: Person regains decision-making capacity (power not exercisable)
Revocation by the person with capacity, resignation, or VCAT revocation

Death of the person: no treatment decisions remain. The Act has no express provision; after death, tissue donation authority passes to the senior available next of kin under the Human Tissue Act 1982.

notes.text: A medical treatment decision maker may consent, before death, to ante-mortem procedures that support donation after death.
The decision maker may access health information relevant to the decision.

Advance care directives: any person with decision-making capacity, including a child, may give an advance care directive. It comes into force when signed and lasts until any expiry date or revocation, and a later directive revokes an earlier one. An applicable instructional directive is given effect directly. The decision maker must first consider any values directive. Powers are subject to limits in the appointment document.
The 2016 Act commenced on 12 March 2018. It replaced medical treatment powers previously given under enduring powers of attorney (medical treatment) and enduring powers of guardianship.

roles.name: Medical treatment decision maker (statutory hierarchy)
roles.summary: If no appointed decision maker is available, a VCAT guardian with medical treatment power comes next. If there is none, the decision maker is the first of these who is in a close and continuing relationship with the person and is reasonably available, willing and able: spouse or domestic partner, then primary carer, then the oldest adult child, parent or adult sibling. This person acts only while the person lacks capacity.

roles.name: Guardian appointed by VCAT
roles.summary: VCAT may appoint a guardian for the personal matters specified in an order. It must be satisfied that, because of disability, the person lacks decision-making capacity for those matters, needs a guardian, and that the order will promote their wellbeing. The guardian cannot manage the estate after death. VCAT must reassess the order within 12 months and at least every 3 years.

roles.name: Executor (grant of probate)
roles.summary: The executor named in a valid will takes authority from the will at death. The Supreme Court, or its registrar, issues a grant of probate that confirms the authority. On the grant, real estate vests in the executor from the date of death. Divorce revokes a former spouse's appointment unless the will shows otherwise. Marriage revokes the whole will, except a will made in contemplation of that marriage.

states.label: Testator has died; executor may act on the will but has not obtained probate
Appointment revoked, renounced, removed, or administration complete

transitions.event: Testator's divorce (appointment of former spouse revoked)
Supreme Court or registrar grants probate
Executor renounces, dies without proving, or does not prove after citation

roles.name: Administrator of a deceased estate (letters of administration)
roles.summary: If there is no will, or no executor willing and able to act, the Supreme Court (or registrar) grants administration. Before a grant, an intestate's estate vests in State Trustees. For estates under the indexed maximum monetary value, State Trustees may file a notice instead of applying for a grant. It is then taken to hold the grant 14 days after the notice is published.

assigned.event: Court or registrar grants administration (including with will annexed)

starts.event: On the grant; title to real estate vests as from death

ends.event: Court discharges or removes administrator
Estate fully administered

states.label: Intestate: estate vests in State Trustees pending a grant
Administration granted (or deemed granted to State Trustees under s 79)

transitions.event: State Trustees gives notice for a small estate; deemed grant 14 days after publication
conditions: Estate value estimated not to exceed the s 71(1A) maximum monetary value ($137,210 from 1 July 2026)

roles.name: Recipient of a small estate payment without a grant
localNames: payment or transfer without production of a grant of representation
roles.summary: A person holding money or personal property of a deceased person worth no more than the threshold amount may pay or transfer it without asking for a grant. The recipient may be the surviving spouse or domestic partner, a child, or any other person who appears to be entitled. The threshold is $25,000 or a higher CPI-indexed amount declared each year: $34,310 from 1 July 2026. The holder decides whether to pay. The recipient is not appointed and gets no power over the rest of the estate.

assigned.event: No appointment. The holder chooses to pay a person who has legal capacity and appears to be entitled.

starts.event: On payment or transfer after death

ends.event: Payment made. The recipient stays answerable to anyone with a claim against the estate.

notes.text: There is no waiting period and no affidavit procedure. The section protects the paying holder: a good-faith payment is a complete discharge. It does not require anyone to pay.

states.label: Holder pays or transfers property within threshold

transitions.event: Holder pays within threshold without requiring grant
conditions: Money or personal property not more than threshold amount
Recipient has legal capacity and appears entitled

transitions.event: Payment complete; holder discharged if in good faith

roles.name: Senior available next of kin (tissue donation)
roles.summary: Victoria uses opt-in consent. A hospital designated officer may authorise removal after death if the deceased consented in writing, or orally during their last illness before two witnesses. Otherwise the senior available next of kin may consent, unless the deceased objected. The order is spouse or domestic partner, then adult child, then parent, then adult sibling. Next of kin may also give consent while the person is unconscious before death.

assigned.event: By statutory definition at death (no appointment)

starts.event: After death, where the deceased has not objected; or while the person is unconscious before death (acted on only after death)

ends.event: Tissue removed or decision made; if the person recovers consciousness the pre-death indication cannot be acted on

notes.text: The deceased's own written consent, or oral consent during the last illness before two witnesses, is sufficient authority by itself. The designated officer then must tell the senior available next of kin.
Unusual rule: if the designated officer cannot find next of kin after reasonable inquiry and has no reason to believe the deceased objected, removal may be authorised without consent (s 26(1)(e)).
Before death, a medical treatment decision maker may consent to ante-mortem procedures for later donation.

states.label: Person unconscious before death; next of kin may indicate consent
After death: senior available next of kin may consent
Deceased objected in writing, or orally in last illness before two witnesses: next-of-kin consent not available

transitions.event: Designated officer has reason to believe deceased objected
Consent given or refused; removal authorised

roles.name: Person entitled to arrange disposal of remains (executor at common law; applicant for interment or cremation authorisation)
roles.summary: No Victorian statute says who controls disposal of a body. The Cemeteries and Crematoria Act 2003 lets 'a person who wishes' remains to be interred or cremated apply to the cemetery trust. The trust may require consent from the holder of the right of interment. At common law the executor, or where none the person with the best claim to administration, has the right to possession of the body for disposal.

assigned.event: Executor named in will (common law); otherwise the person entitled to administration

ends.event: Body buried or cremated

notes.text: If the deceased and relatives cannot pay, the Magistrates' Court or a coroner may order a cemetery trust to inter or cremate free of charge.
Funeral wishes of the deceased are not legally binding at common law in Victoria (law reform context only).

states.label: Executor/likely administrator holds right to possession for disposal; applicant seeks authorisation

transitions.note: Victorian authority (Dow v Hoskins [2003] VSC 206; Keller v Keller (2007) 15 VR 667) is described in the VLRC paper but could not be read on an official host (AustLII blocks automated access). Re Gray is cited as persuasive Australian authority.

transitions.event: Applicant obtains interment or cremation authorisation from cemetery trust
conditions: Medical practitioner certificate plus BDM notice, or coroner's release order

roles.name: Authorised representative / legal representative under the Health Records Act 2001
roles.summary: For a living person who cannot consent or request access, an authorised representative may exercise their Health Records Act rights to the extent needed for the representative's functions. Authorised representatives include a guardian, an enduring attorney, a medical treatment decision maker or an administrator. The Act protects deceased persons for 30 years after death. During that period a legal representative (executor with probate, or administrator) exercises the deceased's rights.

assigned.event: Derived from another role (guardian, enduring attorney, medical treatment decision maker, administrator; after death, executor with probate or administrator)

starts.event: When the individual is incapable of consenting or requesting access (living); on grant of probate or administration (deceased)

ends.event: Underlying authority ends or individual regains capacity
Individual has been dead for more than 30 years: Act no longer applies

notes.text: A legal representative's consent is void if they know or believe it does not accord with wishes the deceased expressed in life and did not withdraw.

states.label: Individual capable, or no underlying authority
Representative exercises Health Records Act rights

transitions.event: Individual dies: living-person authorised representative role ends
After death: executor with probate or administrator exercises rights

poaDurableByDefault.note: A general non-enduring power does not survive incapacity. A power endures only if made in the prescribed enduring form under Part 4.

springingPoaAllowed.note: The principal may specify any time, circumstance or occasion, including loss of capacity, for all matters or a specified matter. The default is on making.

poaRegistrationBeforeUse.note: No registration requirement; effective on execution in prescribed form and acceptance by attorney.

healthAgentStartsOn.note: An appointed medical treatment decision maker's appointment is in force from the date made, but a medical treatment decision is needed only when the person lacks decision-making capacity for that treatment. No clinician certificate or registration is required.

supportedDecisionMakingStatute.name: Powers of Attorney Act 2014 (Vic) Part 7 (supportive attorney appointments, in operation 1 September 2015); Medical Treatment Planning and Decisions Act 2016 (Vic) Part 3 Div 3 (support person); Guardianship and Administration Act 2019 (Vic) Part 4 (supportive guardianship and supportive administration orders)

digitalAssetsFiduciaryStatute.name: None found. The Administration and Probate Act 1958, Powers of Attorney Act 2014 and Guardianship and Administration Act 2019 (current authorised versions) contain no provision on digital assets or online accounts.

onlineToolsRecognisedInLaw.note: No Victorian statute recognises platform legacy-contact or inactive-account tools.

organDonationModel.name: Human Tissue Act 1982 (Vic): the deceased's own consent, or senior available next of kin consent absent objection

smallEstateWithoutGrant.note: Under s 31A a holder may pay money or personal property up to the threshold without a grant. The threshold is the greater of $25,000 and a CPI-indexed amount declared each year: $34,310 from 1 July 2026. Separately, State Trustees may administer estates up to the s 71 maximum monetary value ($137,210 from 1 July 2026) by notice, with a deemed grant after 14 days (s 79).

probateGrantName.note: Executors obtain a grant of probate. Otherwise a grant of administration (letters of administration), from the Supreme Court or its registrar of probates. The Act calls both a 'grant of representation'.

deceasedPersonalDataProtected.note: The Health Records Act 2001 (Vic) applies to deceased individuals for 30 years after death, with rights exercised by the executor or administrator. The Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014 (Vic) defines personal information without referring to deceased persons (not analysed further). Commonwealth Privacy Act status is covered in the national-layer file.

healthAgentPostDeathAuthority.note: An enduring power of attorney is revoked on death and cannot authorise managing the estate. Medical treatment decision-maker powers concern treatment of a living person. After death, tissue consent goes to the senior available next of kin, health-records rights go to the legal representative, and disposal goes to the executor.
